title: WHY DID JESUS TALK ABOUT PEOPLE WHO “MADE THEMSELVES EUNUCHS” FOR THE KINGDOM?
paragraphs:
WHY DID JESUS TALK ABOUT PEOPLE WHO “MADE THEMSELVES EUNUCHS” FOR THE KINGDOM?
One of Jesus’ Most Shocking Statements Was Never Permission to Mutilate Your Body—It Was a Radical Declaration That Christ Can Become More Precious Than Marriage, Sex, Romance, and Every Dream You Thought You Needed to Be Whole
There are verses people underline.
There are verses people put on coffee mugs.
And then there are verses people quietly hope nobody asks them to explain.
Matthew 19:12 is one of those verses.
Jesus says:
“εἰσὶν γὰρ εὐνοῦχοι…”
“For there are eunuchs…”
And then He says something even more startling:
“καὶ εἰσὶν εὐνοῦχοι οἵτινες εὐνούχισαν ἑαυτοὺς διὰ τὴν βασιλείαν τῶν οὐρανῶν.”
Literally, the Greek speaks of eunuchs who “made themselves eunuchs because of the kingdom of heaven.”
Then Jesus finishes:
“ὁ δυνάμενος χωρεῖν χωρείτω.”
“The one who is able to receive this, let him receive it.”
Matthew 19:12.
Read casually, it sounds shocking.
Read carelessly, it can sound horrifying.
But read it in context...
and something breathtaking begins to emerge.
Jesus was not giving His followers instructions for mutilating their bodies.
He was confronting something much deeper.
Something that reaches into our loneliness.
Our sexuality.
Our marriages.
Our singleness.
Our secret cravings.
Our fear of being unwanted.
Our desperate need to have somebody tell us, “I choose you.”
And perhaps most painfully...
our tendency to ask another human being to give us the identity only Jesus Christ can give.
Before we go any further, you need to see what happened immediately before these strange words left the mouth of Jesus.
The Pharisees had approached Him with a question about divorce.
Jesus answered by taking them back to creation.
He spoke of male and female.
He spoke of marriage.
He spoke of two becoming one flesh.
He said that what God has joined together, human beings should not tear apart.
Then the disciples reacted.
And their reaction is almost painfully human.
“If such is the case of a man with his wife, it is better not to marry.”
In other words...
If marriage is really this serious...
maybe staying single is easier.
And that is when Jesus begins talking about eunuchs.
That context changes everything.
Jesus is answering a conversation about marriage and remaining unmarried.
He says not everyone can receive this teaching, “but only those to whom it is given.”
Then He describes three different circumstances.
Some are eunuchs from birth.
Some were made eunuchs by other people.
And some, Jesus says, “made themselves eunuchs” for the sake of the kingdom of heaven.
The Greek word is εὐνοῦχοι — eunouchoi — the plural of εὐνοῦχος, eunouchos.
Historically, a eunuch could refer to a man whose sexual capacity had been physically altered, often within royal or court settings.
So Jesus deliberately chooses startling language.
But notice what He does not say.
He does not command everyone to become a eunuch.
He does not tell His disciples to injure themselves.
He does not establish bodily mutilation as a requirement for entering the kingdom.
Instead, in the immediate context of the disciples saying it might be better “not to marry,” Jesus speaks of a life in which someone relinquishes marriage for the kingdom.
That is why many Christian interpreters have historically understood the third category figuratively as voluntary celibacy or singleness devoted to God rather than literal self-castration.
And suddenly the strange saying becomes intensely personal.
Because Jesus is talking about surrender.
The kind nobody applauds.
The kind that happens when following Christ costs you something you genuinely wanted.
Maybe you have spent years asking God for a spouse.
You watched friends get married.
Then younger friends.
Then people you prayed for.
You smiled in wedding photographs while something inside you quietly whispered:
“When will it be me?”
You went home to a silent room.
Put your phone on the table.
And wondered whether God had forgotten your address.
Maybe that is not your story.
Maybe you are married, but there is another desire you keep negotiating with God about.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
Pornography you keep deleting and returning to.
An emotional affair nobody knows exists.
A sexual compromise you have renamed “love” because calling it sin would require surrender.
A fantasy you feed because reality feels empty.
A secret life hidden behind worship songs, Christian posts, Bible verses, and Sunday smiles.
And somewhere beneath all of it is one terrifying question:
“Jesus... if You ask me to surrender this too, will You really be enough?”
That is where Matthew 19 stops being an unusual Bible passage.
It becomes a mirror.
Because Christianity is not fundamentally the promise that Jesus will give us every earthly thing we desire.
Christianity is the announcement that in Jesus Christ we have found Someone worth surrendering everything to.
Marriage is good.
Sex within God’s design for marriage is good.
Family is good.
Human companionship is good.
But none of them is God.
And whenever a good gift becomes something we cannot imagine obeying Jesus without possessing, that gift has begun competing with the Giver.
That is why these words are so uncomfortable.
Jesus is destroying the lie that romantic fulfillment is the highest form of human existence.
Our culture repeatedly tells us that if nobody desires you romantically, something essential is missing.
If nobody sleeps beside you, you must be incomplete.
If you are unmarried, you are waiting for your “real life” to begin.
If you do not experience sexual fulfillment, you cannot possibly flourish.
Jesus refuses that story.
The most complete human being who ever walked this earth was Jesus Christ.
And Jesus was unmarried.
Think about that.
The Man who showed us humanity without sin did not need marriage to validate His humanity.
He did not need sexual experience to become complete.
He did not need romantic approval to know who He was.
At His baptism, before the public miracles, before Calvary, before the crowds had decided what they thought about Him, the Father declared His love for His Son.
Identity came from the Father.
Not from romance.
And perhaps somebody reading this has spent years begging another person to give you what only God can give.
“You matter.”
“You are wanted.”
“You have value.”
“You belong.”
So you accepted treatment you should never have accepted.
You crossed boundaries you once promised God you would never cross.
You returned to somebody who repeatedly wounded you because loneliness felt worse than dysfunction.
You gave your body hoping somebody would finally give you their heart.
You compromised conviction because you were terrified that obedience might leave you alone.
Listen carefully.
Jesus is not mocking your longing.
The God who created companionship understands loneliness better than you understand it yourself.
But Christ loves you too much to let your loneliness become your lord.
Sometimes surrender sounds less like thunder...
and more like deleting a number.
Closing a browser.
Ending a secret conversation.
Walking away from a relationship that keeps dragging you from Christ.
Choosing another lonely Friday night rather than returning to something God rescued you from.
Sometimes holiness feels like grief before it feels like freedom.
And perhaps that is why Jesus says:
“ὁ δυνάμενος χωρεῖν χωρείτω.”
Let the one who can receive it receive it.
This is not a casual teaching.
It is costly.
And Scripture does not teach that every Christian must remain unmarried.
The Bible honors marriage.
But Scripture also refuses to treat singleness as spiritual failure.
Paul later speaks similarly in 1 Corinthians 7.
Marriage can be a gift.
Singleness can also be a gift.
Neither saves you.
Neither makes Jesus love you more.
Neither replaces the Gospel.
The center is Christ.
Always Christ.
Because here is where this passage becomes even more beautiful.
Jesus did not merely ask people to surrender.
He surrendered Himself.
Before you ever gave anything up for Christ...
Christ gave Himself for you.
The One speaking about sacrifice would eventually walk toward Jerusalem.
Toward betrayal.
Toward abandonment.
Toward nails.
Toward blood.
Toward a cross.
Jesus did not stand safely outside human suffering telling wounded people to try harder.
He entered our suffering.
He carried our sin.
He bore judgment.
He was rejected so sinners could be reconciled to God.
And this is where Christianity differs radically from self-improvement.
The Gospel is not:
“Clean yourself up enough and perhaps God will accept you.”
The Gospel is that sinners who could never cleanse themselves are invited to repent and trust in the crucified and risen Christ.
Grace does not pretend sin is harmless.
Grace takes sin so seriously that the Son of God went to the cross.
But grace also says your scandal does not have to become your final chapter.
Maybe your sexual history is messy.
Maybe your marriage collapsed.
Maybe you committed adultery.
Maybe pornography has controlled years of your life.
Maybe you have slept with people whose names you wish you could erase from your memory.
Maybe you were used.
Maybe you used others.
Maybe you crossed lines you swore you never would.
Maybe there are things in your past you cannot even say aloud without feeling shame crawl up your throat.
The Gospel does not ask you to pretend those chapters never happened.
It announces that Jesus Christ can redeem sinners whose chapters cannot be rewritten by human hands.
Repentance does not mean mutilating yourself.
It means turning from sin toward Christ.
Grace does not mean Jesus approves of everything we have done.
Grace means the sinner who comes to Him does not have to remain imprisoned by what he or she has done.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is a new identity.
There is resurrection life.
There is a Savior.
And His name is Jesus.
Perhaps the most radical “eunuch for the kingdom” application for some readers is not lifelong celibacy.
Perhaps it is finally saying:
“Jesus, nothing gets to own me except You.”
Not pornography.
Not lust.
Not my boyfriend.
Not my girlfriend.
Not my spouse.
Not my loneliness.
Not my sexual past.
Not my desire to be desired.
Not my fear of dying unmarried.
Not the person who abandoned me.
Not the person I cannot stop thinking about.
Not even the dream I have prayed about for twenty years.
Jesus...
You are Lord.
That is Christianity.
Not merely adding Jesus to your desires.
Surrendering your desires to Jesus.
And strangely...
that surrender is where freedom begins.
Because when Christ becomes your treasure, another human being no longer carries the impossible responsibility of becoming your savior.
You can love without worshiping.
You can marry without making marriage your identity.
You can remain single without believing your life is unfinished.
You can experience desire without allowing desire to become your master.
You can grieve what God has not given while still worshiping the God who gave Himself.
And if you fall?
Run back to Christ.
Not away.
Confess.
Repent.
Get into the light.
Ask mature believers for help.
Cut off access to what repeatedly feeds your sin.
Stop protecting the thing that is destroying you.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace opens the prison door.
And maybe this article found you while you are exhausted from fighting.
Maybe everybody thinks you are strong.
But God knows.
God knows about the nights.
God knows about the browser history.
God knows about the texts.
God knows about the memories.
God knows about the loneliness.
God knows about the person you still miss.
God knows how many times you promised, “Never again.”
And God knows you failed again.
Do not confuse conviction with an invitation to despair.
Bring the truth into the light.
There is a cross for sinners.
There is mercy for the repentant.
There is power in the risen Christ.
There is still a road home.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, do not manufacture a religious answer.
Be honest.
If you are still fighting for purity when part of you wants to give up, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If loneliness has been exhausting your spirit, simply comment, “pray for me.”

And if Christ has already been restoring parts of your life you thought were beyond redemption, tell somebody what He has done. Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person needed to read tonight.
Not because every sentence will be easy to hear, but because temptation has a strange way of making us forget truths we were certain about yesterday.
Not as a performance of spirituality.
It does not.
Not because giving money earns salvation.
It cannot.
Christ alone saves.

But if this ministry is helping people encounter Scripture, understand the Gospel, return to Christ, and grow as disciples, financial support is one practical way believers can help that work continue and reach others.
If you want to support the mission and go deeper with us:
But please remember this...
A Christian page cannot save you.
A library of thousands of Christian books cannot save you.
A pastor cannot save you.
Your sexual purity cannot save you.
Your marriage cannot save you.
Your singleness cannot save you.
Your good behavior cannot save you.
Jesus saves.
And perhaps that is the deepest meaning hiding beneath this strange, uncomfortable saying about eunuchs.
The kingdom of heaven is so valuable that surrendering something precious is not ultimately losing everything.
Because when you have Christ...
you have found the Treasure.
So if Jesus asks for the relationship...
give it to Him.
If He asks for the secret habit...
bring it into the light.
If He asks you to wait...
wait with Him.
If He gives you marriage...
honor Him in it.
If He gives you a season of singleness...
do not waste it believing your life has not begun.
If He calls you to costly obedience...
remember the scarred hands of the One doing the calling.
Those hands surrendered more for you than you will ever surrender for Him.
And one day, when every temporary longing has fallen silent, nobody who belongs to Christ will stand before Him regretting that Jesus became their greatest treasure.
The thing you are terrified to place in His hands may be the very thing keeping you from discovering how deeply those hands can hold you.
